hooks.text: A multi-ton NASA telescope pivots in seconds without human commands.
Why would a NASA telescope turn itself without asking ground control?
Most space telescopes take days to move, but this one pivots instantly.

title: The Space Telescope That Hunts on Machine Instinct
description: NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory can pivot its entire multi-ton body in under a minute to catch fleeting cosmic explosions. Launched in 2004, it revolutionized how astronomers study the dying universe.

beats.text: Most missions wait days for human planning, but Swift launched in 2004 to act alone.

beats.text: It carries three co-aligned instruments to catch gamma-ray flashes that last mere seconds.

beats.text: The mission was named for the swift bird, which pivots mid-flight to rapidly change direction.
beats.visual: Close up photograph of a common swift bird in flight, 2015

beats.text: A mask of fifty-two thousand lead tiles calculates the coordinates of the blast.

beats.text: Within one hundred seconds, the spacecraft autonomously slews its entire body to focus its lens.
beats.visual: diagram of Swift spacecraft rotating in Earth orbit, 2004

beats.text: This caught a dying star thirteen billion light-years away, when the universe was six hundred thirty million years old.
beats.visual: discovery image of afterglow from GRB 090423, 2009

beats.text: Built for a two-year mission, the observatory spent two decades hunting these flashes.
